program graph patch operations

To replace text inside one function without retyping the body, use --replace-in-fn (Edit semantics):
  $ zero patch . --replace-in-fn greet --old 'return 1' --new 'return 2'
--old must match the body text zero view --fn <name> prints exactly once; a missing or non-unique
match fails with the occurrence count. Inline --old/--new accept \n escapes; --old-file/--new-file
read the text from a file or - (stdin) for multi-line replacements.

To replace one whole function body, use --replace-fn with --body-file.
--body-file - reads the body rows from stdin, so a heredoc does the whole edit in one call:
  $ zero patch . --replace-fn greet --body-file - <<'EOF'
  check world.out.write("hello agent\n")
  EOF
The body holds only the new body rows in canonical projection syntax, exactly what
zero view --fn <name> prints between the signature braces. No header, no end marker.

structural rewrite by example (cross-cutting edits expressed once):
  zero patch . --rewrite 'bnCmp($A, $B) == 0' --to 'bnEq($A, $B)'
Pattern and template are canonical projection expressions; $A, $B bind arbitrary subtrees and
the same metavariable twice must match equal subtrees. Default is a dry run listing each site
as file fn:handle with rendered before/after; --apply rewrites every site in one batch with one
revalidation pass, and --fn <name> scopes matching to one function. Expression-level patterns only;
unsupported subtree kinds are skipped and counted.

Node handles come from zero view --fn <name> --handles or zero query --fn <name> --handles;
short forms (#55ae, #8b..a5) and full ids both work. replaceExpr swaps one expression subtree:
aimed at a statement handle it replaces that statement's expression (a let initializer, condition,
or return value), so changing a value, operator, or condition is a one-line --op. Multiple --op
flags batch into one patch with a single revalidation pass.
